extracted.intended_audience: Syracuse University community; students, alumni, and aspiring cartoonists/comedians
extracted.subtask_description: A profile-style piece offering career and craft insights from Bob Mankoff about becoming a successful cartoonist/comic, emphasizing persistence, practice, education, voice, and audience alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment, practice, failure, and luck
rubrics_metrics.description: “Becoming a great comedian or cartoonist doesn’t happen overnight. As with many professions, it takes tremendous commitment and practice, a bit of failure and some luck along the way.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame a career as requiring long-term commitment and repeated practice; expect failures and require perseverance; acknowledge role of chance. No specific scoring guidance, but this is presented as foundational to success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce large volume and persistently submit work
rubrics_metrics.description: Mankoff submitted hundreds to thousands of cartoons — e.g., did 27 early cartoons, then submitted around 2,000 cartoons to The New Yorker before getting published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes iteration and volume: keep creating many pieces, continue submitting despite rejections. Example: persistence over decades led to ~1,000 New Yorker cartoons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop and ‘invent’ a distinctive comedic identity
rubrics_metrics.description: College allowed him to 'invent yourself' and he knew 'I was funny and creative' — developing a personal presence and persona was key to his emergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formative experiences (college, environments) to try out and refine a unique voice/persona. The article treats self-invention as an active craft element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use humor as a subversive force to establish identity
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The power of humor as a subversive force that lets you have an identity within an institution.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply humor to challenge norms or stand out in institutions (e.g., campus), using subversion strategically to gain recognition and shape one's role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage education and interdisciplinary study to shape comic sensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Mankoff studied psychology at Syracuse and used that liberal arts experience as a launchpad, which 'molded his comedic identity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal study (including non-art subjects like psychology) and a liberal arts background can inform comedic perspective and craft; treat education as content and method development, not just credentialing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from classroom assignments and seek affirmation/feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: In English 101 he wrote a humorous essay that was read aloud after positive teacher feedback, which affirmed and encouraged his comedic path.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage actively with coursework and instructor feedback as opportunities to test material and build confidence; early positive responses can validate direction and skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft gags that align with audience feelings and timing (relatability & topicality)
rubrics_metrics.description: He attributes the popularity of 'How About Never—Is Never Good for You?' to aligning with people’s feelings about meetings at that time: 'I think it hit that moment and it’s a good gag.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful cartoons/gags often resonate because they capture a shared sentiment or cultural moment; aim for relatability and timing when choosing themes and punchlines.
